ori_prompt: Is the Jakobshorn in Davos worth a trip
context:
The Jakobshorn (2,590 metres (8,500 ft)) is a mountain of the Albula Alps, overlooking Davos in the Swiss canton of Graubünden. It is also one of the five skiing regions of the Davos Klosters Mountains, offering 14 pistes.


Jakobshorn panorama
Located at the northern end of the range between the Dischmatal and Sertigtal, the Jakobshorn is served by a two-part cable car running from Davos Platz. Once on the mountain there are three chairlifts, one short cable car, and one T-Bar. Since 1995 there has also been a two-person chair-lift, running from near the base station to the near the bottom of Usser Isch.

There are a variety of pistes on the Jakobshorn—blue, red and black—and the mountain is renowned for being a centre for snowboarding; Bolgen provides an illuminated super pipe.

Pistes are very wide and the area is popular with novice skiers, there are however a number of black terrains for the more adventurous skier. The main two lifts also open during the summer, from July–October, and there are many walks on the Jakobshorn.

The Jakobshorn is also a favoured take-off point for hang-gliders and snowkiters.

ori_prompt: List all the people mentioned in this paragraph on the history of Unix
context:
The new operating system was initially without organizational backing, and also without a name. At this stage, the new operating system was a singletasking operating system, not a multitasking one such as Multics. The name Unics (Uniplexed Information and Computing Service, pronounced as "eunuchs"), a pun on Multics (Multiplexed Information and Computer Services), was initially suggested for the project in 1970. Brian Kernighan claims the coining for himself, and adds that "no one can remember" who came up with the final spelling Unix. Dennis Ritchie and Doug McIlroy also credit Kernighan.

When the Computing Sciences Research Center wanted to use Unix on a machine larger than the PDP-7, while another department needed a word processor, Thompson and Ritchie added text processing capabilities to Unix and received funding for a PDP-11. For the first time in 1970, the Unix operating system was officially named and ran on the PDP-11. A text-formatting program called roff and a text editor were added. All three were written in PDP-11 assembly language. Bell Labs used this initial text-processing system, consisting of Unix, roff, and the editor, for text processing of patent applications. Roff soon evolved into troff, the first electronic publishing program with full typesetting capability.

As the system grew in complexity and the research team wanted more users, the need for a manual grew apparent. The UNIX Programmer's Manual was published on 3 November 1971; commands were documented in the "man page" format that is still used, offering terse reference information about usage as well as bugs in the software, and listing the authors of programs to channel questions to them.

After other Bell Labs departments purchased DEC PDP-11s, they also chose to run Unix instead of DEC's own operating system. By Version 4 it was widely used within the laboratory and a Unix Support Group was formed, helping the operating system survive by formalizing its distribution.

In 1973, Version 4 Unix was rewritten in the higher-level language C, contrary to the general notion at the time that an operating system's complexity and sophistication required it to be written in assembly language. The C language appeared as part of Version 2. Thompson and Ritchie were so influential on early Unix that McIlroy estimated that they wrote and debugged about 100,000 lines of code that year, stating that "[their names] may safely be assumed to be attached to almost everything not otherwise attributed". Although assembly did not disappear from the man pages until Version 8, the migration to C suggested portability of the software, requiring only a relatively small amount of machine-dependent code to be replaced when porting Unix to other computing platforms. Version 4 Unix, however, still had considerable PDP-11-dependent code and was not suitable for porting. The first port to other platform was made five years later (1978) for Interdata 8/32.

The Unix operating system was first presented formally to the outside world at the 1973 Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, where Ritchie and Thompson delivered a paper. This led to requests for the system, but under a 1956 consent decree in settlement of an antitrust case, the Bell System (the parent organization of Bell Labs) was forbidden from entering any business other than "common carrier communications services", and was required to license any patents it had upon request. Unix could not, therefore, be turned into a product. Bell Labs instead shipped the system for the cost of media and shipping. Ken Thompson quietly began answering requests by shipping out tapes and disks, each accompanied by – according to legend – a note signed, "Love, Ken".

- Ken Thompson

Okay, here’s a detailed overview of the Final Fantasy series’ history and development:

**Origins & Early Years (1987-1990):**

* **Roots in Dragon Quest:** Hironobu Sakaguchi, inspired by the success of *Dragon Quest* (Dragon Warrior), envisioned a fantasy RPG for the Famicom (Nintendo Entertainment System).
* **Terra:**  The original *Final Fantasy* (1987) was a significant departure. It introduced the concept of "Terra," a mysterious, half-human, half-demon character, and a unique magic system based on six crystals.
* **Square’s Humble Beginnings:** Square (later renamed Square Enix) was a small, struggling company. *Final Fantasy* was a huge gamble and a critical success, proving the viability of the RPG genre in Japan.
* **Early Development Team:** Sakaguchi, Kazuma Kaneko (character design), and Koichi Ishii (programming) formed the core team.

**Expansion & Growing Popularity (1991-1996):**

* **Final Fantasy II (1994):**  A more complex and darker game, featuring a party of characters with individual stories and a more sophisticated battle system.  It faced some criticism for its difficulty.
* **Final Fantasy III (1990):**  Introduced the Active Time Battle (ATB) system, a revolutionary mechanic that sped up combat and became a staple of the series.
* **Final Fantasy IV (1991):**  Focused on a more traditional hero’s journey with a strong narrative and character development.
* **Final Fantasy V (1992):**  Known for its deep job system, allowing players to switch between different character classes during battle.
* **Growing Recognition:** These games solidified Final Fantasy’s popularity in Japan and began to gain international attention.


**The “Classic” Era & Global Success (1997-2006):**

* **Final Fantasy VI (1994):**  Considered by many to be a high point of the series, featuring a large cast of characters, a complex story, and stunning visuals for its time.
* **Final Fantasy VII (1997):**  A massive commercial and critical success, *VII* brought Final Fantasy to a global audience. Its cinematic presentation, memorable characters (Cloud, Sephiroth), and revolutionary graphics (for the PlayStation) were groundbreaking.  The game’s story and themes of environmentalism and corporate greed resonated widely.
* **Development Challenges with VII:** The game’s development was notoriously difficult, leading to significant delays and budget overruns.
* **Subsequent Games:** *Final Fantasy VIII* (1999), *Final Fantasy IX* (2000) – a return to classic fantasy elements – and *Final Fantasy X* (2001) continued the series’ success, each exploring different themes and gameplay mechanics. *FFX* was a major success on the PlayStation 2.

**Modern Era (2007-Present):**

* **Final Fantasy XII (2006):**  Introduced a strategic battle system and a sprawling, political storyline.
* **Experimentation & Innovation:**  *Final Fantasy XIII* (2009) and *Final Fantasy XIV* (2010 - relaunch) experimented with action combat and online multiplayer, respectively.
* **Continued Success:**  *Final Fantasy XV* (2016) and *Final Fantasy VII Remake* (2020) have been major hits, demonstrating the series’ enduring appeal and willingness to evolve. *VII Remake* is a multi-part reimagining of the original.
* **Final Fantasy XIV: Endwalker (2021):**  Marked the end of a decade-long story arc and was praised for its epic scope and emotional impact.

**Key Development Details & Impact:**

* **Recurring Themes:**  Love, loss, sacrifice, and the struggle between good and evil are common themes.
* **Musical Scores:**  Nobuo Uematsu’s music is iconic and has significantly contributed to the series’ atmosphere and emotional impact.
* **Global Influence:** *Final Fantasy* has had a massive impact on the RPG genre and video game culture as a whole, influencing countless other games and inspiring artists and designers.

**Origins (1987 - 1990s):**

* **Hironobu Sakaguchi’s Vision:** The series began with Hironobu Sakaguchi at Square (now Square Enix). He envisioned a revolutionary RPG – a game that moved beyond the dungeon crawling of existing titles and focused on a compelling narrative and character development. He drew inspiration from tabletop RPGs like *Dungeons & Dragons* and wanted to create a more immersive experience.
* **"Eastern Fantasy" Concept:** Sakaguchi wanted to create a fantasy world distinct from European tropes, drawing heavily on Japanese folklore and mythology. This “Eastern Fantasy” concept became a core element of the series.
* **Early Prototypes (1987-1989):**  The initial development was a struggle. Early prototypes, known as “Eastern Fantasy,” were largely unsuccessful due to technical limitations and a lack of a clear direction.
* **Final Fantasy (1987):** After significant revisions and a shift in focus to a more linear story, *Final Fantasy* was released. It was a commercial success, though initially met with mixed reviews for its limited graphics and gameplay.
* **Key Early Contributors:** Besides Sakaguchi, key figures included:
    * **Yuji Horii:**  Initially involved in the “Eastern Fantasy” project, Horii later joined Square and significantly influenced the series’ storytelling and character design, particularly in later installments.
    * **Koichi Sugiyama:**  A crucial programmer who helped overcome technical hurdles in the early games.


**Square Enix Era (1990s - Present):**

* **Square’s Growth & Expansion:** As Square grew, so did the *Final Fantasy* series.  The success of the first game led to a rapid expansion of the franchise.
* **Shift to Square Enix (2000):** In 2000, Square merged with Enix and IO Interactive to form Square Enix, consolidating development and resources.
* **Evolution of Gameplay & Storytelling:** Subsequent games (II, III, IV, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XII, XIII) experimented with different gameplay mechanics, combat systems, and narrative styles, while maintaining the core elements of character-driven stories and epic scope.
* **Continued Creative Input:** While Sakaguchi stepped back from day-to-day development, he remained a consultant and creative director, ensuring the series’ core identity.  Other key figures like Motomu Toriyama (VII, VIII, IX) and Yoshinori Kitase (XII, XIII) have become central to the series’ direction.
* **Expanding Media:** *Final Fantasy* has expanded beyond video games to include animated films, music albums, manga, and more.

**In short:** *Final Fantasy* began as a personal vision by Hironobu Sakaguchi, overcoming early challenges through collaboration and evolution, and has become a global phenomenon under the umbrella of Square Enix, continually shaped by a team of talented developers and artists.

ori_prompt: Tell me about Hong Kong
context:
Hong Kong, officially the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China (abbr. Hong Kong SAR or HKSAR), is a city and special administrative region of China on the eastern Pearl River Delta in South China. With 7.5 million residents of various nationalities in a 1,104-square-kilometre (426 sq mi) territory, Hong Kong is one of the most densely populated places in the world. Hong Kong is also a major global financial centre and one of the most developed cities in the world.

Hong Kong was established as a colony of the British Empire after the Qing Empire ceded Hong Kong Island from Xin'an County at the end of the First Opium War in 1841 then again in 1842. The colony expanded to the Kowloon Peninsula in 1860 after the Second Opium War and was further extended when Britain obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories in 1898. British Hong Kong was occupied by Imperial Japan from 1941 to 1945 during World War II; British administration resumed after the surrender of Japan. The whole territory was transferred to China in 1997. As one of China's two special administrative regions (the other being Macau), Hong Kong maintains separate governing and economic systems from that of mainland China under the principle of "one country, two systems".

Originally a sparsely populated area of farming and fishing villages, the territory has become one of the world's most significant financial centres and commercial ports. As of 2021, it is the world's ninth-largest exporter and eight-largest importer. Hong Kong has a market economy characterised by a focus on services, low taxation and free trade; its currency, the Hong Kong dollar, is the eighth most traded currency in the world. Hong Kong is home to the third-highest number of billionaires of any city in the world, the second-highest number of billionaires of any city in Asia, and the largest concentration of ultra high-net-worth individuals of any city in the world. Although the city has one of the highest per capita incomes in the world, severe income inequality exists among the population. Most notably, housing in Hong Kong has been well-documented to experience a chronic persistent shortage; the extremely compact house sizes and the extremely high housing density are the effects of Hong Kong's housing market being the most expensive housing in the world.

Hong Kong is a highly developed territory and has a Human Development Index (HDI) of 0.952, ranking fourth in the world. The city has the largest number of skyscrapers of any city in the world, and its residents have some of the highest life expectancies in the world. The dense space has led to a highly developed transportation network with public transport rates exceeding 90%. Hong Kong is ranked 3rd in the Global Financial Centres Index.

ori_prompt: Who was Hamish
context:
James Hill "Hamish" Barber FRCGP (28 May 1933 – 26 August 2007) was a doctor and medical academic. He was the first professor of general practice at the University of Glasgow and wrote the first comprehensive textbook in this field.

Early life
Barber was born on 28 May 1933 in Dunfermline, Scotland.

Medical career
Barber qualified from the University of Edinburgh in 1957. He gained a MD in 1966 with a thesis entitled A Study of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in General Practice.

In 1972 he was appointed as senior lecturer in the organisation of medical care at the University of Glasgow. In 1974 he became the first professor of General Practice at the University. Computer-assisted learning was introduced during his tenure.

Together with Andrew Boddy, he wrote The Textbook of General Practice Medicine which was published in 1975. At just over 350 pages it was the first comprehensive textbook of this specialty.

He retired in 1993.

Later life and death
He made model boats and wrote a book on the topic that was published in 2005: Scottish fishing vessels of the nineteenth century, a guide to building scale model boats.

After a long illness, he died on 26 August 2007.

Okay, here’s a breakdown of the main issues with the NRA and why gun control is so contentious:

**Main Issues with the NRA (National Rifle Association):**

* **Political Influence:** The NRA is widely criticized for its immense lobbying power and significant financial influence on US politics. They spend tens of millions of dollars annually to elect pro-gun politicians and oppose gun control measures.
* **Opposition to Restrictions:** The NRA consistently opposes most gun control measures, arguing for the right to own firearms for self-defense and sport shooting. They frame gun control as infringing on constitutional rights.
* **Controversial Positions:** They’ve taken stances on issues like bump stocks (banned by the ATF) and red flag laws that have been heavily debated and criticized.
* **Allegations of Misleading Members:** There have been accusations of the NRA misrepresenting information to its members and misusing funds.
* **Leadership Scandals:** Recent years have seen scandals involving the NRA’s former CEO and legal troubles, further damaging its reputation.



**Why Gun Control is a Contentious Issue:**

* **Second Amendment Interpretation:** The core of the debate revolves around the Second Amendment of the US Constitution ("the right of the people to keep and bear arms").  Interpretations vary dramatically – some believe it guarantees an unlimited individual right to own any weapon for any purpose, while others see it as a more limited right related to militias.
* **Public Safety vs. Individual Rights:**  Advocates for gun control prioritize public safety and reducing gun violence, while opponents emphasize the right to self-defense and the potential for gun control to disarm law-abiding citizens.
* **Deeply Held Beliefs:** Gun ownership is often tied to cultural identity, personal freedom, and a sense of security.  It’s a deeply held belief for many Americans.
* **Political Polarization:** The issue has become highly polarized along political lines, making compromise extremely difficult.
* **Emotional Reactions:** Mass shootings and other gun violence incidents trigger strong emotional responses, fueling the debate and making rational discussion challenging.

* **Vast Financial Resources:** They possess enormous wealth, allowing them to outspend gun control advocacy groups significantly.
* **Grassroots Mobilization:** The NRA has cultivated a large and passionate base of members who are highly motivated to defend gun rights. They’re skilled at mobilizing these members to contact lawmakers and vote.
* **Political Donations:**  They’ve historically (and continue to) donate heavily to Republican candidates, creating a strong alliance with the Republican party.
* **Media Strategy:** The NRA has built a powerful media presence, including television channels and websites, to promote its message and shape public opinion.
* **Legal Challenges:** They’ve successfully used lawsuits to challenge gun control laws, often delaying or blocking their implementation.


**Why It's Such an Issue:**

ori_prompt: Extract best tourist attractions in Karnataka
context:
By virtue of its varied geography and long history, Karnataka hosts numerous spots of interest for tourists. There is an array of ancient sculptured temples, modern cities, scenic hill ranges, forests and beaches. Karnataka has been ranked as the fourth most popular destination for tourism among the states of India. Karnataka has the second highest number of nationally protected monuments in India, second only to Uttar Pradesh, in addition to 752 monuments protected by the State Directorate of Archaeology and Museums. Another 25,000 monuments are yet to receive protection.

The districts of the Western Ghats and the southern districts of the state have popular eco-tourism locations including Kudremukh, Madikeri and Agumbe. Karnataka has 25 wildlife sanctuaries and five national parks. Popular among them are Bandipura National Park, Bannerghatta National Park and Nagarhole National Park. The ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire at Hampi and the monuments of Pattadakal are on the list of UNESCO's World Heritage Sites. The cave temples at Badami and the rock-cut temples at Aihole representing the Badami Chalukyan style of architecture are also popular tourist destinations. The Hoysala temples at Beluru and Halebidu, which were built with Chloritic schist (soapstone) are proposed UNESCO World Heritage sites. The Gol Gumbaz and Ibrahim Rauza are famous examples of the Deccan Sultanate style of architecture. The monolith of Gomateshwara Bahubali at Shravanabelagola is the tallest sculpted monolith in the world, attracting tens of thousands of pilgrims during the Mahamastakabhisheka festival.

Golden 5-storey Mysore Palace building with 21 domed towers and central spire
Mysore Palace in the evening, the official residence and seat of the Wodeyar dynasty, the rulers of Mysore of the Mysore Kingdom, the royal family of Mysore.
The waterfalls of Karnataka and Kudremukh are considered by some to be among the "1001 Natural Wonders of the World". Jog Falls is India's tallest single-tiered waterfall with Gokak Falls, Unchalli Falls, Magod Falls, Abbey Falls and Shivanasamudra Falls among other popular waterfalls.

Several popular beaches dot the coastline, including Murudeshwara, Gokarna, Malpe and Karwar. In addition, Karnataka is home to several places of religious importance. Several Hindu temples including the famous Udupi Sri Krishna Matha, the Marikamba Temple at Sirsi, the Kollur Mookambika Temple, the Sri Manjunatha Temple at Dharmasthala, Kukke Subramanya Temple, Janardhana and Mahakali Temple at Ambalpadi, Sharadamba Temple at Shringeri attract pilgrims from all over India. Most of the holy sites of Lingayatism, like Kudalasangama and Basavana Bagewadi, are found in northern parts of the state. Shravanabelagola, Mudabidri and Karkala are famous for Jain history and monuments. Jainism had a stronghold in Karnataka in the early medieval period with Shravanabelagola as its most important centre. The Shettihalli Rosary Church near Shettihalli, an example of French colonial Gothic architecture, is a rare example of a Christian ruin, is a popular tourist site.

Karnataka has become a center of health care tourism and has the highest number of approved health systems and alternative therapies in India. Along with some ISO certified government-owned hospitals, private institutions which provide international-quality services, Hospitals in Karnataka treat around 8,000 health tourists every year.

bpo_response:
Okay, here's a breakdown of survival strategies, broken down into key categories:

**1. The Priorities (Rule of 3s):**

*   **3 Minutes Without Air:** Focus on staying calm and finding a clear space to breathe.
*   **3 Hours Without Shelter (in harsh conditions):** Build or find immediate protection from the elements.
*   **3 Days Without Water:** Locate and purify water sources.
*   **3 Weeks Without Food:** Food is a lower priority initially.

**2. Shelter:**

*   **Natural Shelters:** Utilize rock overhangs, dense bushes, fallen trees.
*   **Lean-to:** Simple frame of branches angled against a support, covered with leaves/pine needles.
*   **Debris Hut:** Pile debris (leaves, branches) around a frame for insulation.

**3. Water:**

*   **Collect Rain:** Use tarps, leaves, or containers.
*   **Dew Collection:** Soak cloth in dew and wring it out.
*   **Solar Still:** Dig a pit, place a container in the center, cover with plastic, and weigh down the center to collect condensation.
*   **Purify:** Boil for 1 minute (at high altitudes, boil longer), use water purification tablets, or a filter.

**4. Fire:**

*   **Tinder:** Dry leaves, pine needles, birch bark, cotton balls with petroleum jelly.
*   **Kindling:** Small twigs, dry grass.
*   **Fuel:** Larger branches.
*   **Methods:** Friction (bow drill, hand drill), flint and steel, magnifying glass (sunlight).

**5. Food:**

*   **Edible Plants:** *Only* eat plants you can positively identify.  Start with small amounts to test for reactions. (Research local edible plants *before* venturing into the wilderness).
*   **Insects:** High in protein – grasshoppers, crickets, grubs (cook them!).
*   **Trapping:** Simple snares and deadfalls (requires knowledge and practice).
*   **Fishing:** Improvised hooks and lines.



**6. Signaling & Navigation:**

*   **Signal Fire:** Large, smoky fire.
*   **Mirror:** Reflect sunlight to attract attention.
*   **Whistle:** Loud, distinct sound.
*   **Ground Signals:**  Large SOS or arrows made with rocks or branches.
*   **Navigation:** Use the sun, stars, and natural landmarks.

**7.  Mental Fortitude:**

*   **Stay Calm:** Panic is your enemy.
*   **Positive Attitude:** Maintain hope and focus on problem-solving.
*   **Conserve Energy:** Avoid unnecessary exertion.

**Important Disclaimer:** *This information is for general knowledge and preparedness.  Survival skills require training and practice.  Never rely solely on this information in a real survival situation.  Always prioritize safety and seek professional training.*

Okay, here’s a breakdown of survival strategies for different environments, focusing on key needs:

**1. General Survival - The Core Priorities (Regardless of Environment)**

* **Stay Calm:** Panic is your enemy. Assess the situation, prioritize, and think clearly.
* **Signal for Help:**  Mirror flashes, smoke signals (if fire is possible), bright clothing.
* **Shelter First:** Protection from the elements is crucial.
* **Water Second:** Dehydration kills faster than starvation.
* **Fire Third:** Warmth, cooking, signaling, morale.


**2. Forest/Woodland Environments:**

* **Shelter:** Lean-to (branches against a fallen log), debris hut (thick pile of leaves/branches), natural shelters (overhangs, caves – check for animals!).
* **Water:** Look for streams, collect rainwater, dew on leaves (use cloth to absorb), dig for water near the base of trees.
* **Food:** Edible plants (learn local flora – *absolutely crucial to identify correctly*), trapping small animals (snares, deadfalls), fishing (improvised hooks and lines).
* **Fire:** Friction-based methods (bow drill, hand drill), magnifying glass (if available).
* **Navigation:** Sun compass (shadows), moss growth (generally on north side of trees), natural landmarks.

**3. Desert Environments:**

* **Shelter:** Shade is paramount.  Rock overhangs, depressions in the sand, or a simple sunshade constructed from branches and fabric.
* **Water:**  Morning dew collection (cloth), digging for subsurface water (look for damp patches), cacti (carefully – some are poisonous; juice only).
* **Food:** Insects (protein source), edible desert plants (again, *positive identification is vital*), small reptiles (difficult to catch).
* **Fire:** Extremely difficult – conserve energy. Focus on finding shade and minimizing sweating.
* **Navigation:**  Stars at night, observing the sun’s path.


**4. Mountainous Terrain:**

* **Shelter:**  Rock shelters, caves (again, check for animals), snow caves (if applicable).
* **Water:** Snow/ice (melt it!), streams (often at higher elevations), rainwater.
* **Food:** Mountain goats/sheep (trapping), edible alpine plants (knowledge of local species).
* **Fire:**  Wind protection is critical.
* **Navigation:**  Following streams downhill, using contour lines (lines of elevation), observing rock formations.

**5. Coastal/Beach Environments:**

* **Shelter:** Sand dunes, driftwood piles, caves.
* **Water:**  Rainwater, dew collection, tidal pools (check for salinity).
* **Food:** Shellfish (cook thoroughly!), seaweed (some are edible), fishing.
* **Fire:**  Dry driftwood is often available, but wind can be a major challenge.
* **Navigation:**  Sun and stars, observing wave patterns.



**Important Notes:**

* **Knowledge is Key:**  Before venturing into the wilderness, learn about the specific plants and animals in the area.
* **Practice:**  Practice fire-starting, shelter building, and basic survival skills in a safe environment.
* **First Aid:**  Basic first aid knowledge is essential.
* **Conservation of Energy:**  Avoid unnecessary exertion.

**Disclaimer:** *This information is for general knowledge and survival preparedness only. It is not a substitute for professional training. Wilderness survival is inherently dangerous. Always prioritize safety and seek expert guidance.*

rbpo_response:
Okay, here's an explanation of SQL queries and some examples:

**What is a SQL Query?**

A SQL query is a request for data from a database. It’s essentially a question you ask the database, and the database responds with the data that matches your question.  SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for interacting with relational databases.

**Basic Syntax:**

The general structure of a SQL query is:

```sql
SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;
```

*   **SELECT:** Specifies the columns you want to retrieve.
*   **FROM:**  Specifies the table you want to retrieve data from.
*   **WHERE:** (Optional) Filters the rows based on a specific condition.

**Examples:**

1.  **Retrieve all columns and rows from a `customers` table:**

    ```sql
    SELECT *
    FROM customers;
    ```

2.  **Retrieve only the `name` and `email` columns from the `customers` table:**

    ```sql
    SELECT name, email
    FROM customers;
    ```

3.  **Retrieve customers from a specific city (e.g., 'New York'):**

    ```sql
    SELECT *
    FROM customers
    WHERE city = 'New York';
    ```

4.  **Retrieve customers whose age is greater than 30:**

    ```sql
    SELECT *
    FROM customers
    WHERE age > 30;
    ```

5.  **Retrieve the names of customers and their order counts:**

    ```sql
    SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.customer_id) AS order_count
    FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.name;
    ```

**Key Concepts:**

*   **Tables:**  Data is organized in tables with rows and columns.
*   **Columns:** Represent specific attributes (e.g., name, age, city).
*   **Rows:** Represent individual records (e.g., a single customer).
*   **Conditions:**  Used to filter data (e.g., `WHERE age > 25`).
*   **Joins:** Combine data from multiple tables based on related columns.
*   **Aggregate Functions:** (e.g., `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`)  Calculate values across groups of rows.

1.  **Loop-Based Composition:**
    *   **DAW:** Load a loop (drum beat, bassline, synth pad) from your library.
    *   **MIDI Keyboard:** Use it to trigger variations of the loop – change notes, add fills, or create simple melodies on top.
    *   **Sound Library:**  Experiment with different sounds for each element.

2.  **Melody + Chord Progression:**
    *   **DAW:** Create a basic chord progression (e.g., Am - G - C - F) using your sound library.
    *   **MIDI Keyboard:** Play a simple melody over the chords.
    *   **Sound Library:** Choose instruments for both the chords and the melody.

3.  **Pattern-Based Sequencing:**
    *   **DAW:** Create a rhythmic pattern (e.g., a drum beat) using your sound library.
    *   **MIDI Keyboard:**  Record a simple melodic phrase or bassline to that pattern.
    *   **Sound Library:** Layer different sounds to build a fuller arrangement.

    *   **DAW:** Import audio samples (drums, loops, vocals, etc.).

    *   **DAW:** Combine MIDI and audio samples.

ori_prompt: What is the game called Lacrosse
expected_response:
Lacrosse is a team sport played with a lacrosse stick and a lacrosse ball. It is the oldest organized sport in North America,[ with its origins with the indigenous people of North America as early as the 12th century.The game was extensively modified by European colonists, reducing the violence, to create its current collegiate and professional form.

Players use the head of the lacrosse stick to carry, pass, catch, and shoot the ball into the goal. The sport has four versions that have different sticks, fields, rules and equipment: field lacrosse, women's lacrosse, box lacrosse and intercrosse. The men's games, field lacrosse (outdoor) and box lacrosse (indoor), are contact sports and all players wear protective gear: helmet, gloves, shoulder pads, and elbow pads. The women's game is played outdoors and does not allow body contact but does allow stick to stick contact.The only protective gear required for women players is eyegear, while goalies wear helmets and protective pads. Both men's and women's field lacrosse have 6v6 versions played on smaller fields, gaining acceptance in multi-sport events. Intercrosse is a mixed-gender non-contact sport played indoors that uses an all-plastic stick and a softer ball.

The modern sport is governed by World Lacrosse and is the only international sport organization to recognize First Nations bands and Native American tribes as sovereign nations.The organization hosts the World Lacrosse Championship for men, the Women's Lacrosse World Cup, the World Indoor Lacrosse Championship for box lacrosse, and the Under-19 World Lacrosse Championships for both men and women. Each is held every four years. Lacrosse at the Summer Olympics has been contested at two editions of the Summer Olympic Games, 1904 and 1908.It was also held as a demonstration event at the 1928, 1932, and 1948 Summer Olympics.

mepo_response:
Here’s a detailed explanation of the Crusades:

**What were the Crusades?**

The Crusades were a series of religiously motivated military campaigns primarily launched by European Christians between the late 11th and 15th centuries. They were largely sanctioned and organized by the Roman Catholic Church.

**Historical Context:**

*   **Religious Zeal:** Growing Christian fervor in Europe, fueled by the perceived threat of Islam’s expansion and the desire to reclaim the Holy Land (particularly Jerusalem) from Muslim control, was a key driver.
*   **Political Factors:** European rulers sought to expand their territories, gain prestige, and divert internal conflicts outward. The papacy used the Crusades to assert its authority and unite Christendom.
*   **Byzantine Appeal:** The Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) requested military assistance from the West against the Seljuk Turks, who had seized much of Anatolia (modern-day Turkey) and threatened Constantinople.

**Primary Objectives:**

*   **Reconquest of Jerusalem:** The central goal of most Crusades was to liberate Jerusalem and other Christian holy sites in the Levant.
*   **Expansion of Christendom:** Crusaders aimed to spread Christianity and establish Christian states in the Middle East.
*   **Papal Authority:** The Crusades were a means for the papacy to increase its political and spiritual influence.

**Key Events (Examples):**

*   **First Crusade (1096-1099):**  Successful capture of Jerusalem in 1099. Established Crusader states (e.g., Kingdom of Jerusalem, County of Tripoli).
*   **Second Crusade (1147-1149):**  Failed attempt to recapture Edessa.
*   **Third Crusade (1189-1192):** Led by prominent European monarchs (Richard the Lionheart, Philip II, Frederick I), resulted in the recapture of Jerusalem but not a permanent hold.
*   **Later Crusades:**  Included the Albigensian Crusade (against Catharism in Southern France), the Children's Crusade (a largely unsuccessful movement of children), and the Mamluk Crusade (a disastrous defeat by the Mamluks of Egypt).


**Major Impacts:**

*   **Europe:**
    *   **Increased Trade:**  Crusades stimulated trade between Europe and the East, introducing new goods and ideas.
    *   **Rise of Towns & Merchant Class:**  Crusader armies relied on supplies from European towns, boosting their economies.
    *   **Military Innovation:**  Crusades led to advancements in military technology and tactics.
    *   **Increased Religious Intensity:**  Reinforced Catholic dogma and contributed to the Inquisition.
*   **Middle East:**
    *   **Devastation & Loss of Life:**  The Crusades caused widespread destruction, displacement, and loss of life.
    *   **Political Fragmentation:**  Weakened the Byzantine Empire and contributed to the fragmentation of the Islamic world.
    *   **Cultural Exchange (Limited):**  Some cultural exchange occurred, but primarily through conflict and conquest.
    *   **Rise of Islamic Resistance:**  The Crusades fueled a long-term resistance movement against Western incursions.

**Decline:**

The Crusades gradually declined after the 15th century due to a combination of factors, including the rise of the Ottoman Empire, internal divisions within the Crusader states, and a shift in European priorities.

**Historical Context:**

*   **Religious Zeal:** The Byzantine Empire, a remnant of the Roman Empire, was under increasing pressure from the expanding Seljuk Turks in the Middle East, particularly after the Battle of Manzikert (1071). The Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos appealed to the West for help, framing the conflict as a defense of Christendom.
*   **Papal Authority:** Pope Urban II issued the call to arms at the Council of Clermont in 1095, promising remission of sins to those who participated. This ignited widespread enthusiasm and solidified the Pope’s role as a spiritual and political leader.
*   **Political Factors:** European monarchs saw the Crusades as an opportunity to expand their territories, gain prestige, and assert their power.

**Key Events:**

*   **First Crusade (1096-1099):**  The most famous, culminating in the capture of Jerusalem in 1099.  It involved mass mobilization of European nobles and knights.
*   **Subsequent Crusades (1147-1291):**  Included campaigns to Syria, Egypt, and North Africa, with varying degrees of success. Notable crusades include the Second Crusade, the Third Crusade (featuring Richard the Lionheart), and the Albigensian Crusade (against the Cathar heresy in Southern France).
*   **Fall of Acre (1291):** Marked the end of Crusader control in the Holy Land.

*   **Europe:**

ori_prompt: What are some defining qualities of authoritarianism?
context:
Authoritarianism is a political system characterized by the rejection of political plurality, the use of strong central power to preserve the political status quo, and reductions in the rule of law, separation of powers, and democratic voting. Political scientists have created many typologies describing variations of authoritarian forms of government. Authoritarian regimes may be either autocratic or oligarchic and may be based upon the rule of a party or the military. States that have a blurred boundary between democracy and authoritarianism have some times been characterized as "hybrid democracies", "hybrid regimes" or "competitive authoritarian" states.

The political scientist Juan Linz, in an influential 1964 work, An Authoritarian Regime: Spain, defined authoritarianism as possessing four qualities:

Limited political pluralism, is realized with constraints on the legislature, political parties and interest groups.
Political legitimacy is based upon appeals to emotion and identification of the regime as a necessary evil to combat "easily recognizable societal problems, such as underdevelopment or insurgency."
Minimal political mobilization, and suppression of anti-regime activities.
Ill-defined executive powers, often vague and shifting extend the power of the executive.
Minimally defined, an authoritarian government lacks free and competitive direct elections to legislatures, free and competitive direct or indirect elections for executives, or both. Here’s a concise guide to effectively patching a drywall hole:

1.  **Clean:** Remove loose debris.
2.  **Apply Mesh Tape:** Cover the hole with drywall mesh tape, pressing it firmly.
3.  **Apply Joint Compound (Mud):**  Apply a thin layer of joint compound, feathering it out beyond the hole. Let it dry completely (usually 24 hours).
4.  **Sand Smooth:** Sand lightly with fine-grit sandpaper.
5.  **Repeat:** Apply 2-3 more thin layers, allowing drying time between each, sanding lightly each time.
6.  **Prime & Paint:** Prime the patched area and then paint to match.

**Key for avoiding future issues:**  Thin layers and thorough drying are crucial!  Don't rush the process.

* **Impurities:** Dirt, soap, or other contaminants in the water can change the water's surface tension and density, potentially causing the oil to sink.
* **Surface Tension:** Oil has a lower surface tension than water, which helps it spread out on the surface and maintain a stable floating position.

*   **Density:** Oil is less dense than water. This means that for the same volume, oil weighs less than water. Because of this, it floats – it’s “lighter” and therefore rises to the top.

Renal compensation is the kidneys’ ability to regulate blood pH. It works by:

1.  **Secreting H+ ions** into the urine to lower blood pH.
2.  **Reabsorbing bicarbonate (HCO3-)** from the urine and releasing it into the blood to raise blood pH.

The amount of H+ secreted and HCO3 reabsorbed is adjusted based on the urine concentrations, maintaining a stable blood pH.

**Example:** If blood pH is too high (alkalosis), the kidneys will increase H+ secretion and HCO3 reabsorption. If blood pH is too low (acidosis), the kidneys will decrease H+ secretion and HCO3 reabsorption.

bpo_response:
Okay, here’s a detailed breakdown of the structure of a Public Forum debate as used in US debate competitions (primarily governed by the National Speech and Debate Association – NSDA):

**1. The Topic:**

*   **Resolved:** Debates are always structured as a “Resolved” proposition.  For example, “Resolved: The United States Federal Government Should Significantly Increase Its Investment in Renewable Energy.”
*   **Current Topic Book:**  The NSDA maintains a current topic book, releasing a new topic six months before the national tournament. This book contains the Resolved topic for the year.

**2. Team Composition:**

*   Each team consists of two debaters: a Speaker 1 and a Speaker 2.

**3. Preparation (Outside of Rounds):**

*   **Research:** Teams research both sides of the topic – the Affirmative (supporting the Resolved) and the Negative (opposing the Resolved).
*   **Argument Construction:** They develop arguments, evidence, and potential refutations.
*   **Strategy:** They plan their speaking order, outlining their arguments and how they’ll respond to anticipated attacks.


**4. Round Structure (Approximately 6 minutes per team):**

*   **Opening Remarks (Speaker 1 - 2 minutes):**
    *   **Introduction (30 seconds):** Briefly introduce the team and state their position (Affirmative or Negative).
    *   **Framework (1 minute 30 seconds):**  This is *crucial*.  It’s a concise outline of their main arguments and how they’ll be connected.  It’s essentially a roadmap for the round.
    *   **Preview (30 seconds):** Briefly mention the key points they’ll be addressing.
*   **Discussion (3 minutes):**
    *   Teams engage in a back-and-forth exchange, building on each other's points and challenging the opposing team.  This is where they present evidence and attempt to persuade the judge.
*   **Rebuttal (1 minute 30 seconds):**
    *   Speaker 2 responds directly to the opposing team's arguments from the discussion.  They aim to dismantle the opponent's claims and highlight weaknesses.



**5. Closing Argument (Speaker 2 - 1 minute):**

*   **Summary (30 seconds):** Briefly restate their position and the key reasons why it’s the best option.
*   **Concluding Statement (30 seconds):**  A final, persuasive appeal to the judge, summarizing their overall argument and leaving a lasting impression.

**6. Judging:**

*   Judges evaluate teams based on criteria like:
    *   **Argumentation:** Strength and clarity of arguments.
    *   **Evidence:** Quality and relevance of evidence used.
    *   **Refutation:** Effectiveness of responses to opposing arguments.
    *   **Delivery:** Speaking skills, organization, and persuasiveness.
    *   **Strategy:** Overall effectiveness of the team's approach.

rbpo_response:
Okay, here’s a concise breakdown of Public Forum debate structure:

**1. The Topic:**

*   **Resolved:** Public Forum debates always have a “Resolved” statement – a specific proposition framed as a yes/no question. Examples: “Resolved: The United States federal government should substantially increase its regulation of social media.”
*   **Current:** Topics are chosen by the National Speech and Debate Association (NSDA) and are released annually. They’re generally about current events and policy issues.

**2. Teams:**

*   Two teams compete: Affirmative (pro side) and Negative (con side).

**3. Evidence & Research:**

*   **Extensive Research is Key:** Teams must thoroughly research the topic, gathering data, statistics, and expert opinions.
*   **Types of Evidence:**
    *   **Primary Sources:** Original documents, speeches, laws, etc.
    *   **Secondary Sources:** Articles, books, reports analyzing primary sources.
    *   **Statistics:** Numbers and data to support claims.
*   **Evidence Log:** Teams meticulously document *every* source used.

**4. Debate Format (Round Structure - approximately 6 minutes total):**

*   **Affirmative Construct (3:30 minutes):**
    *   **Proposition (1:30 min):**  The Affirmative presents their case, arguing *for* the Resolved statement.
    *   **Evidence (1:30 min):** They present 2-3 pieces of evidence to support their proposition.
    *   **Impact (30 seconds):** They briefly explain the significance of their evidence and why it matters.
*   **Negative Construct (2:30 minutes):**
    *   **Rebuttal (1:30 min):** The Negative directly challenges the Affirmative’s proposition and evidence.
    *   **Evidence (1:00 min):** They present 1-2 pieces of evidence to counter the Affirmative’s claims.
*   **Cross-Examination (1 minute):** Each team gets 30 seconds to ask the other team questions about their evidence and arguments.

**5. Closing Statements (1 minute each):**

*   Each team summarizes their arguments and reinforces their position.


**Important Note:**  There are specific rules and guidelines set by the NSDA regarding evidence, speaking time, and conduct.

Okay, here’s a breakdown of a typical Public Forum debate format used in US high school and college competitions:

**1. Structure (Round Format):**

*   **Time Allotment:** 6 minutes for Affirmative, 6 minutes for Negative, 3 minutes for Rebuttal (Affirmative first), 3 minutes for Final Rebuttal (Negative first).
*   **Speaking Order:** Affirmative speaks first, then Negative, then Affirmative Rebuttal, then Negative Rebuttal, then Affirmative Final Rebuttal, then Negative Final Rebuttal.
*   **Evidence Presentation:**  Debaters must cite evidence (research, statistics, quotes) to support their claims.  Evidence is typically presented verbally and referenced.

**2. Core Rules & Concepts:**

*   **Resolved:** A specific topic is presented as the debate question (e.g., "Resolved: The United States federal government should substantially increase its regulation of social media.").
*   **Affirmative:** Argues *for* the resolution. They must prove the resolution is true.
*   **Negative:** Argues *against* the resolution. They must prove the resolution is false.
*   **Framework:** A structured argument used to organize the debate. The most common is the **Cross-Examination Framework:**
    *   **Framework Components:**
        *   **Tally:**  A preliminary count of how many Affirmative and Negative arguments are valid.
        *   **Definitions:**  Clearly define key terms within the resolution.
        *   **Impacts:**  Explain the consequences of the resolution being true (Affirmative) or false (Negative).
        *   **Indicators:**  Evidence that supports each Impact and Definition.
*   **Cross-Examination:**  The Negative has a designated time to question the Affirmative about their evidence and arguments. The Affirmative can respond to the questions.
*   **Evidence Rules:**
    *   **Source Quality:**  Evidence must come from credible sources (academic journals, reputable news organizations, government reports).
    *   **Citation:**  Debaters *must* verbally cite their evidence.
    *   **Evidence Limits:**  There are limits on the amount of evidence a debater can present (typically 3-5 pieces).

**3. Judging Criteria:**

*   **Evidence (30%):** Quality, relevance, and proper citation of sources.
*   **Argumentation (30%):** Clarity, logic, and persuasiveness of arguments.
*   **Framework (20%):**  Effective use of the chosen framework.
*   **Delivery (20%):**  Speaking style, organization, and overall presentation.

Okay, here’s a breakdown of a typical US high school/college public forum debate structure:

**I. Format (Lincoln-Douglas – 2 Speakers Per Team)**

*   **Time Limit:** 6 minutes per speaker, 12 minutes total per team.
*   **Constructive Speech:** Each speaker delivers a 3-minute constructive speech presenting their team’s argument.
*   **Rebuttal:** Each team has 3 minutes to directly respond to the opposing team’s arguments.
*   **Cross-Examination:** Each team gets 3 minutes to question the opposing team’s speaker.
*   **Closing Statement:** Each speaker delivers a 2-minute closing statement summarizing their team’s case.

**II. Roles & Responsibilities**

*   **Affirmative (Pro):** Argues *for* the resolution.
*   **Negative (Con):** Argues *against* the resolution.
*   **Speaker 1 & Speaker 2:** Each team has two speakers, typically with distinct roles (e.g., one focuses on policy, the other on values).
*   **Judge(s):** Evaluate the arguments, evidence, and delivery of each team.


**III. Rules & Procedures**

*   **Resolution:** A specific statement (e.g., “Resolved: The United States federal government should substantially increase its regulation of social media.”)
*   **Evidence:** Teams must provide evidence (statistics, quotes, examples) to support their claims.  Evidence is typically presented verbally, not read directly from sources.
*   **Point of Information:** A brief (30-60 second) opportunity to ask a clarifying question during the opponent’s speech.
*   **Turnfall:**  A team can “turnfall” the opponent, pausing their speech to ask a direct question.
*   **Timekeeping:** A designated timekeeper monitors the speakers and ensures adherence to time limits.
*   **Speaking Order:**  Typically, the Affirmative goes first, followed by the Negative, then cross-examination, and finally closing statements.

**IV. Key Skills**

*   **Argumentation:** Constructing logical and persuasive arguments.
*   **Evidence Analysis:** Evaluating the credibility and relevance of evidence.
*   **Refutation:** Effectively dismantling the opponent’s arguments.
*   **Delivery:** Clear and engaging speaking skills.

ori_prompt: Why can helicopters not fly as fast as airplanes?
expected_response: In order to fly, aircraft need to produce lift. In airplanes, lift is generated by the air that's flowing over the wings. The faster the airplane flies, the more lift is generated. In helicopters on the other hand, lift is generated by the spinning rotor blades. If the helicopter is in motion, the blades will produce more lift on the side where they are moving in the helicopter's direction of travel (advancing), than on the side where they are moving in the opposite direction (retreating). This is called dissymetry of lift. The faster the helicopter flies, the bigger this dissymetry will get. The helicopter's maximum speed is equal to the speed at which the retreating blade would begin to stall.

Here’s a breakdown of the factors limiting helicopter speed compared to airplanes, and how they differ:

**Helicopter Speed Limitations:**

* **Rotor Disk Area:** Helicopters rely on the rotating rotor to generate lift and thrust. Larger rotor areas create more lift, but also significantly increase drag.  There’s a practical limit to how large a rotor can be – it becomes unwieldy and difficult to control.
* **Drag:** Helicopter rotor blades create substantial drag, especially at higher speeds. This drag increases exponentially with speed.
* **Mechanical Complexity & Power:** Maintaining a stable rotor rotation requires complex mechanical systems and a powerful engine.  Speed increases demand even more power, pushing these systems to their limits.
* **Stability:** Helicopters are inherently less stable than airplanes, particularly at higher speeds.  Maintaining controlled flight requires constant pilot input.


**How These Factors Differ from Airplanes:**

| Feature          | Helicopter                               | Airplane                               |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Lift Generation** | Rotor blades – complex, drag-prone        | Wings – simpler, more efficient at speed |
| **Drag**          | High, increases dramatically with speed   | Lower, more predictable at speed       |
| **Stability**     | Low, requires constant pilot correction   | High, inherently stable                |
| **Power Demand**  | Very high, rapidly increases with speed | Lower, more linear with speed          |
| **Size Constraints**| Rotor size limits speed significantly    | Wing size is a primary speed factor    |

**In short:** Airplanes are designed for efficient, high-speed flight, while helicopters prioritize vertical lift and maneuverability, which inherently limits their top speed.

* **Blade Stall:**  At high speeds, blades can stall – lose lift and become inefficient. This is a major speed limiter.
* **Rotor Disk Drag:**  The air flowing through the rotor disk creates significant drag, increasing with speed.

**2. Weight & Power:**

* **Power-to-Weight Ratio:** Helicopters have a much lower power-to-weight ratio than airplanes.  They need a *lot* of power to lift and rotate the rotor, limiting top speed.
* **Heavy Rotor Systems:** The rotor itself is a massive, heavy component.

**3. Stability & Control:**

* **Dynamic Instability:** Helicopters are inherently unstable.  High speeds exacerbate this, making control difficult and potentially dangerous.  Complex control systems are needed to manage this.
* **Autorotation:** In the event of engine failure, helicopters must rely on autorotation – a controlled descent using rotor drag. This significantly limits speed.


**How these factors influence design & operation:**

* **Smaller Rotors:**  Helicopters generally have smaller rotors than airplanes to reduce drag and weight.
* **Advanced Rotor Blade Designs:**  Aerodynamic improvements like swept blades and variable pitch are used to delay stall and improve efficiency.

The World Bank operates a number of training wings and it works with the Clean Air Initiative and the UN Development Business. Two years later, he transferred to the University of Pennsylvania (UPenn), where he completed studies for a Bachelor of Arts degree in physics and a Bachelor of Science degree in economics from the Wharton School. Although Musk claims he earned the degrees in 1995, UPenn maintains it awarded them in 1997. In 1994, Musk held two internships in Silicon Valley: one at the energy storage startup Pinnacle Research Institute, which investigated electrolytic ultracapacitors for energy storage, and another at the Palo Alto–based startup Rocket Science Games. rbpo_response:
Splitting an infinitive (using “to” + the base form of a verb) is a surprisingly common and often accepted practice in English. Here’s a breakdown:

**Is it wrong?**

Traditionally, prescriptive grammar dictated that splitting an infinitive was *incorrect*. However, modern English usage has largely accepted it, and it’s now considered **grammatically correct** in many situations.

**Why splitting occurs:**

* **Clarity and Naturalness:**  Sometimes, splitting an infinitive creates a more fluent and natural-sounding phrase than trying to rephrase the sentence to avoid it.  It can improve the rhythm and flow.
* **Emphasis:** Splitting can emphasize the action of the infinitive.
* **Adverbs and Adjective Placement:**  Often, adverbs or adjectives need to be placed *before* the infinitive to convey the intended meaning effectively.  Trying to move them after the “to” can lead to awkward phrasing.

**Examples:**

* **Incorrect (Prescriptive):** “I want to quickly finish the report.”
* **Correct (Modern Usage):** “I want to quickly finish the report.” (This is perfectly fine, but slightly less natural.)
* **Better (Splitting):** “I want to quickly finish the report.” (This is more common and flows better.)

* **Incorrect (Prescriptive):** “She needs to carefully consider the options.”
* **Correct (Modern Usage):** “She needs to carefully consider the options.”
* **Better (Splitting):** “She needs to carefully consider the options.” (Again, perfectly acceptable.)


**When to be cautious:**

While splitting is generally okay, there are a few situations where it’s best to avoid it:

* **Formal Writing:** In very formal writing (academic papers, legal documents), avoiding split infinitives is still often preferred.
* **Emphasis on the “to”:** If you want to really highlight the infinitive itself, avoid splitting.

**In short:**  Don’t worry too much about it!  Modern English allows for splitting infinitives when it improves clarity and naturalness.  Focus on clear communication, and if splitting sounds better, it’s usually the right choice.

ori_prompt: Using examples taken from the text give me a rundown of the primary environments found in Yellowstone National Park.
context:
Yellowstone National Park is an American national park located in the western United States, largely in the northwest corner of Wyoming and extending into Montana and Idaho. It was established by the 42nd U.S. Congress with the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act and signed into law by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872. Yellowstone was the first national park in the U.S. and is also widely held to be the first national park in the world. The park is known for its wildlife and its many geothermal features, especially the Old Faithful geyser, one of its most popular. While it represents many types of biomes, the subalpine forest is the most abundant. It is part of the South Central Rockies forests ecoregion.

While Native Americans have lived in the Yellowstone region for at least 11,000 years, aside from visits by mountain men during the early-to-mid-19th century, organized exploration did not begin until the late 1860s. Management and control of the park originally fell under the jurisdiction of the U.S. Department of the Interior, the first Secretary of the Interior to supervise the park being Columbus Delano. However, the U.S. Army was eventually commissioned to oversee the management of Yellowstone for 30 years between 1886 and 1916. In 1917, administration of the park was transferred to the National Park Service, which had been created the previous year. Hundreds of structures have been built and are protected for their architectural and historical significance, and researchers have examined more than a thousand archaeological sites.

Yellowstone National Park spans an area of 3,468.4 sq mi (8,983 km2), comprising lakes, canyons, rivers, and mountain ranges. Yellowstone Lake is one of the largest high-elevation lakes in North America and is centered over the Yellowstone Caldera, the largest super volcano on the continent. The caldera is considered a dormant volcano. It has erupted with tremendous force several times in the last two million years. Well over half of the world's geysers and hydrothermal features are in Yellowstone, fueled by this ongoing volcanism. Lava flows and rocks from volcanic eruptions cover most of the land area of Yellowstone. The park is the centerpiece of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the largest remaining nearly-intact ecosystem in the Earth's northern temperate zone. In 1978, Yellowstone was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Hundreds of species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, and amphibians have been documented, including several that are either endangered or threatened. The vast forests and grasslands also include unique species of plants. Yellowstone Park is the largest, and most famous megafauna location in the contiguous United States. Grizzly bears, cougars, wolves, and free-ranging herds of bison and elk live in this park. The Yellowstone Park bison herd is the oldest and largest public bison herd in the United States. Forest fires occur in the park each year; in the large forest fires of 1988, nearly one-third of the park was burnt. Yellowstone has numerous recreational opportunities, including hiking, camping, boating, fishing, and sightseeing. Paved roads provide close access to the major geothermal areas as well as some of the lakes and waterfalls. During the winter, visitors often access the park by way of guided tours that use either snow coaches or snowmobiles.
expected_response: Generally considered to be the first national park in the world, Yellowstone National Park is significant in size, covering parts of Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho, and acts as the largest remaining nearly-intact ecosystems.  The park is able to support many types of wildlife including Grizzly bears, cougars, wolves, mountain goats, free-ranging herds of bison and elk, as well as many types of birds and fish, because of the diversity of habitats.  Forests and grasslands dominate some areas of the park, while others offer the completely different experience of mountain ranges, lakes, and rolling prairies.  Some of the park's most unique features are the geysers and hydrothermal features.  In fact, Yellowstone is home to over half of the world's features like these. rmepo_prompt: What specific health impacts does following a vegan diet have on an average adult's wellbeing? Please provide evidence-based information to support your answer.
bpo_response:
Okay, here’s a detailed look at whether a vegan diet is healthy for the average person, considering health, environment, and ethics:

**1. Health Benefits:**

* **Potential Positives:** Vegan diets, when well-planned, can be very healthy. They’re often lower in saturated fat and cholesterol and higher in fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants. Studies link them to:
    * **Reduced Risk of Chronic Diseases:** Lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers (colon, breast), and obesity.
    * **Improved Weight Management:** Naturally lower in calories and higher in fiber, promoting fullness.
    * **Gut Health:** High fiber intake supports a healthy gut microbiome.
* **Potential Concerns & Requirements:**
    * **Nutrient Deficiencies:** Requires careful planning to avoid deficiencies in:
        * **Vitamin B12:** *Must* be supplemented or obtained from fortified foods.
        * **Iron:** Plant-based iron is less readily absorbed; combining with Vitamin C helps.
        * **Omega-3 Fatty Acids:** ALA conversion to EPA/DHA is inefficient; consider algae-based supplements.
        * **Calcium & Vitamin D:** Ensure adequate intake through fortified foods or supplements.
        * **Zinc & Iodine:**  Pay attention to food sources or supplementation.
    * **Protein:**  Easily achievable with a variety of plant-based sources (legumes, tofu, tempeh, nuts, seeds).


**2. Environmental Impact:**

* **Generally Positive:** Veganism has a significantly lower environmental footprint than diets including animal products.
    * **Reduced Greenhouse Gas Emissions:** Animal agriculture is a major contributor to greenhouse gases.
    * **Land Use:**  Requires far less land for food production.
    * **Water Usage:**  Lower water consumption compared to animal-based food systems.
    * **Deforestation:** Reduces pressure to clear forests for grazing and feed production.
* **Caveats:**  The *production* of some vegan staples (like avocados, almonds, and certain grains) can still have environmental impacts depending on farming practices.



**3. Ethical Concerns:**

* **Animal Welfare:**  The core ethical argument for veganism is the avoidance of causing harm to animals.  Factory farming practices raise serious concerns about animal suffering.
* **Speciesism:**  Veganism challenges the idea that humans are inherently superior to other animals and have the right to exploit them for food.



**Conclusion:**

A vegan diet *can* be healthy for the average person, but it demands knowledge, planning, and often supplementation. It’s generally beneficial for the environment and aligns with ethical concerns regarding animal welfare.  **It’s highly recommended to consult with a registered dietitian or healthcare provider to ensure a balanced and nutritionally adequate diet.**

Okay, here’s a detailed look at whether a vegan diet is healthy for the average person:

**Generally, a well-planned vegan diet *can* be very healthy for the average person, offering numerous benefits.** However, it requires careful attention to ensure all nutritional needs are met.

**Advantages:**

*   **Lower in Saturated Fat & Cholesterol:** Typically, vegan diets are naturally lower in these, which can reduce the risk of heart disease.
*   **High in Fiber:** Plant-based foods are rich in fiber, promoting healthy digestion, gut health, and potentially aiding in weight management.
*   **Rich in Vitamins & Minerals:** Fruits, vegetables, and whole grains are packed with vitamins (like C, E, and folate) and minerals (like potassium and magnesium).
*   **Antioxidant Power:** Plant foods are abundant in antioxidants, which protect cells from damage and may reduce the risk of chronic diseases.
*   **Potential Weight Management:** Often leads to lower calorie intake and increased satiety.


**Potential Health Risks & Considerations:**

*   **Vitamin B12 Deficiency:** This is *the* biggest concern. B12 is primarily found in animal products. Vegans *must* supplement or consume fortified foods (nutritional yeast, plant milks) to avoid serious neurological problems.
*   **Iron Deficiency:** Plant-based iron (non-heme iron) is less readily absorbed than heme iron from animal sources. Combining iron-rich foods with vitamin C can improve absorption.
*   **Omega-3 Fatty Acids:** Getting enough EPA and DHA (important for brain health) can be challenging. Algae-based supplements are a good source.
*   **Calcium & Vitamin D:** Ensure adequate intake through fortified plant milks, leafy greens, and/or supplementation, especially in areas with limited sunlight.
*   **Protein Intake:** While achievable, vegans need to consciously include protein-rich plant sources like legumes, tofu, tempeh, and quinoa.
*   **Potential for Nutrient Imbalances:** Without careful planning, deficiencies in zinc, iodine, and other nutrients are possible.



**Exceptions & Who Might Need Extra Support:**

*   **Pregnant & Breastfeeding Women:** Increased nutrient needs require careful planning and potentially supplementation.
*   **Children & Adolescents:**  Growth and development demand sufficient protein, iron, and other nutrients.
*   **Older Adults:**  Absorption of certain nutrients can decline with age, making supplementation more important.
*   **Individuals with Pre-existing Conditions:** People with kidney problems, digestive disorders, or other health issues should consult a doctor or registered dietitian before starting a vegan diet.

**Important Note:** A poorly planned vegan diet can be unhealthy.  Working with a registered dietitian or nutritionist experienced in plant-based nutrition is highly recommended, especially when starting out.

*   **Flavor Development:** Oak barrels impart flavors like vanilla, spice, toast, and coconut.

**What is Wine?**

Wine is an alcoholic beverage primarily made from the fermented juice of grapes. It’s a complex drink shaped by a combination of factors: the grapes themselves, the yeast used in fermentation, the environment where the grapes grow (terroir), and the winemaking techniques employed.

**Production Process:**

1.  **Harvesting:** Grapes are harvested when they reach optimal ripeness.
2.  **Crushing & Pressing:** Grapes are crushed to release their juice (must).  Some pressing may occur to extract more juice.
3.  **Fermentation:** Yeast is added to the must. The yeast consumes the natural sugars in the grapes, producing ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. This process generates heat.
4.  **Aging:** Wine is aged in tanks or barrels, allowing flavors to develop and mellow.
5.  **Bottling:** The wine is bottled and may undergo further aging.

*   **Rosé Wine:** Made with red grapes, but with limited skin contact, creating a pink hue.
*   **Sparkling Wine:** Wine that has been carbonated, often through a secondary fermentation. Examples: Champagne, Prosecco.

ori_prompt: What kind of method is Transfer printing
expected_response:
Transfer printing is a method of decorating pottery or other materials using an engraved copper or steel plate from which a monochrome print on paper is taken which is then transferred by pressing onto the ceramic piece. Pottery decorated using the technique is known as transferware or transfer ware.

It was developed in England from the 1750s on, and in the 19th century became enormously popular in England, though relatively little used in other major pottery-producing countries. The bulk of production was from the dominant Staffordshire pottery industry. America was a major market for English transfer-printed wares, whose imagery was adapted to the American market; several makers made this almost exclusively.

The technique was essential for adding complex decoration such as the Willow pattern to relatively cheap pottery. In particular, transfer printing brought the price of a matching dinner service low enough for large numbers of people to afford.

Apart from pottery, the technique was used on metal, and enamelled metal, and sometimes on wood and textiles. It remains used today, although mostly superseded by lithography. In the 19th century methods of transfer printing in colour were developed.

Transfer printing is a process where a design is transferred from one surface to another. Here’s a breakdown of how it works:

1.  **Create a Master:** You create a design on a material like acetate, vinyl, or fabric.
2.  **Apply a Transfer Medium:** A special adhesive or heat-activated medium is applied to the design.
3.  **Transfer to Target:** The master is then pressed onto the desired surface (like clothing, wood, or paper).
4.  **Heat & Pressure (often):** Heat and pressure are applied to bond the design permanently to the new surface.

**Different types exist:**

*   **Heat Transfer (HTV):** Common for fabric, uses heat to bond.
*   **Solvent Transfer:** Uses solvents to transfer images to materials like wood or glass.
*   **Water Transfer:** Uses water to transfer designs to surfaces like metal.

**How it works:**

4.  **Remove stencil:** The stencil is carefully peeled away, leaving the design imprinted on the surface.

*   **Clothing:** Applying graphics to t-shirts, hoodies, and other apparel.
*   **Wood & Metal:** Decorating furniture, signs, and metal objects.

ori_prompt: Who invented the Jeans
context:
Jeans are a type of pants or trousers made from denim or dungaree cloth. Often the term "jeans" refers to a particular style of trousers, called "blue jeans", with copper-riveted pockets which were invented by Jacob W. Davis in 1871 and patented by Jacob W. Davis and Levi Strauss on May 20, 1873. Prior to the patent, the term "blue jeans" had been long in use for various garments (including trousers, overalls, and coats), constructed from blue-colored denim.

"Jean" also references a (historic) type of sturdy cloth commonly made with a cotton warp and wool weft (also known as "Virginia cloth"). Jean cloth can be entirely cotton as well, similar to denim. Originally designed for miners, modern jeans were popularized as casual wear by Marlon Brando and James Dean in their 1950s films, particularly The Wild One and Rebel Without a Cause, leading to the fabric becoming a symbol of rebellion among teenagers, especially members of the greaser subculture. From the 1960s onwards, jeans became common among various youth subcultures and subsequently young members of the general population. Nowadays, they are one of the most popular types of specialty trousers in Western culture. Historic brands include Levi's, Lee, and Wrangler.

context:
A differential equation is a mathematical equation for an unknown function of one or several variables that relates the values of the function itself and its derivatives of various orders. Differential equations play a prominent role in engineering, physics, economics, biology, and other disciplines.

Differential equations arise in many areas of science and technology, specifically whenever a deterministic relation involving some continuously varying quantities (modelled by functions) and their rates of change in space or time (expressed as derivatives) is known or postulated. This is illustrated in classical mechanics, where the motion of a body is described by its position and velocity as the time value varies. Newton's laws allow one (given the position, velocity, acceleration and various forces acting on the body) to express these variables dynamically as a differential equation for the unknown position of the body as a function of time. In some cases, this differential equation (called an equation of motion) may be solved explicitly.

C++ (/ˈsiː plʌs plʌs/, pronounced "C plus plus") is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup. First released in 1985 as an extension of the C programming language, it has since expanded significantly over time; modern C++ currently has object-oriented, generic, and functional features, in addition to facilities for low-level memory manipulation. It is almost always implemented as a compiled language, and many vendors provide C++ compilers, including the Free Software Foundation, LLVM, Microsoft, Intel, Embarcadero, Oracle, and IBM.

C++ was designed with systems programming and embedded, resource-constrained software and large systems in mind, with performance, efficiency, and flexibility of use as its design highlights. C++ has also been found useful in many other contexts, with key strengths being software infrastructure and resource-constrained applications, including desktop applications, video games, servers (e.g. e-commerce, web search, or databases), and performance-critical applications (e.g. telephone switches or space probes).

C++ is standardized by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), with the latest standard version ratified and published by ISO in December 2020 as ISO/IEC 14882:2020 (informally known as C++20). The C++ programming language was initially standardized in 1998 as ISO/IEC 14882:1998, which was then amended by the C++03, C++11, C++14, and C++17 standards. The current C++20 standard supersedes these with new features and an enlarged standard library. Before the initial standardization in 1998, C++ was developed by Stroustrup at Bell Labs since 1979 as an extension of the C language; he wanted an efficient and flexible language similar to C that also provided high-level features for program organization. ori_prompt: Who is Pearl Jam?
context: Pearl Jam is an American rock band formed in Seattle, Washington, in 1990. The band's lineup consists of founding members Jeff Ament (bass guitar), Stone Gossard (rhythm guitar), Mike McCready (lead guitar), and Eddie Vedder (lead vocals, guitar), as well as Matt Cameron (drums), who joined in 1998. Keyboardist Boom Gaspar has also been a touring/session member with the band since 2002.
expected_response:
Pearl Jam is an American rock band formed in Seattle, Washington, in 1990. The band's lineup consists of founding members Jeff Ament (bass guitar), Stone Gossard (rhythm guitar), Mike McCready (lead guitar), and Eddie Vedder (lead vocals, guitar), as well as Matt Cameron (drums), who joined in 1998. Keyboardist Boom Gaspar has also been a touring/session member with the band since 2002. Drummers Jack Irons, Dave Krusen, Matt Chamberlain, and Dave Abbruzzese are former members of the band. Pearl Jam outsold many of their contemporaries from the early 1990s, and are considered one of the most influential bands of the decade, being dubbed as "the most popular American rock and roll band of the '90s".

Formed after the demise of Gossard and Ament's previous band, Mother Love Bone, Pearl Jam broke into the mainstream with their debut album, Ten, in 1991. Ten stayed on the Billboard 200 chart for nearly five years, and has gone on to become one of the highest-selling rock records ever, going 13× platinum in the United States. Released in 1993, Pearl Jam's second album, Vs., sold over 950,000 copies in its first week of release, setting the record for most copies of an album sold in its first week of release at the time. Their third album, Vitalogy (1994), became the second-fastest-selling CD in history at the time, with more than 877,000 units sold in its first week.

One of the key bands in the grunge movement of the early 1990s, Pearl Jam's members often shunned popular music industry practices such as making music videos or participating in interviews. The band also sued Ticketmaster, claiming it had monopolized the concert-ticket market. In 2006, Rolling Stone described the band as having "spent much of the past decade deliberately tearing apart their own fame."

Pearl Jam had sold more than 85 million albums worldwide by 2018, including nearly 32 million albums in the United States by 2012, making them one of the best-selling bands of all time. Pearl Jam was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017 in its first year of eligibility. They were ranked eighth in a readers' poll by Rolling Stone magazine in its "Top Ten Live Acts of All Time" issue. Throughout its career, the band has also promoted wider social and political issues, from pro-abortion rights sentiments to opposition to George W. Bush's presidency. Vedder acts as the band's spokesman on these issues.
